extracted.intended_audience: general readers, tech enthusiasts, developers, and journalists seeking an encyclopedic overview of Apple Intelligence
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic overview of Apple's 'Apple Intelligence' generative AI suite, covering its features, architecture, release timeline, supported devices and languages, privacy claims, integrations, reception, and legal disputes. Useful for readers wanting a comprehensive product-and-policy summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supported devices / hardware requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All iPhones, iPads, and Macs that have an M-series Apple Silicon chip or an A17 Pro or newer chip are supported with iOS 18.1, iPadOS 18.1, and macOS 15.1 respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists supported Mac, iPad, iPhone and Vision Pro models (e.g., MacBook Air/Pro with M1 or later, various iPad Pro/Air models, iPhone 15 Pro/15 Pro Max or later, iPhone 16 or later, Apple Vision Pro (M2) or later). Apple claims the less capable Neural Engine of older chips is not powerful enough; analyst speculation mentions RAM requirements may prohibit older iPhone models.

rubrics_metrics.name: macOS availability restricted to Apple silicon
rubrics_metrics.description: On macOS, Apple Intelligence is available only on Apple silicon Mac computers; Intel-based Mac computers are not supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit platform limitation described in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boot/installation limitation on macOS
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple Intelligence cannot be used on Macs if the operating system is booted off of an external drive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that workarounds exist to circumvent the limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-device plus cloud model architecture and privacy design (Private Cloud Compute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple Intelligence consists of an on-device model as well as a cloud model running on servers primarily using Apple silicon. Apple's cloud models are run entirely on Apple servers with custom Apple silicon hardware built for end-to-end encryption and a Private Cloud Compute platform allegedly designed with user privacy in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article states Apple designed the platform to preserve user privacy, run servers on Apple hardware (not third parties), and ensure the server software matches independently verifiable software accessible to researchers; devices will refuse to connect if there's a software mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party model integration and opt-in privacy controls (ChatGPT integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: ChatGPT integration is opt-in by default, with users being prompted before any data or photos are sent to ChatGPT servers and IP addresses being obscured when requests are sent to OpenAI's servers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using ChatGPT features is free without signing in but limited to a number of GPT-4o requests; paid subscribers can sign in for more requests. The article also notes Apple plans to integrate other models (e.g., Google's Gemini) in the future and reports about privacy-protecting measures around integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and regional availability / localization
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple Intelligence language support expanded across iOS/macOS releases (English initially, then additional English locales, then Chinese (Simplified), Portuguese (Brazil), French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, Vietnamese, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides a version-by-version table of supported languages and notes international release rollout details. It also notes that as of March 2026, Apple Intelligence was not yet available on devices purchased in mainland China or on accounts set to mainland China, and discusses China-specific integration efforts and regulatory review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification/news summary labeling and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Notification summaries for news apps were disabled in iOS 18.3 beta after complaints and a disclaimer was added warning summaries 'may contain errors'; when re-enabled, all news summaries have a 'Summarized by Apple Intelligence' label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts BBC complaints about incorrect summaries, Apple stating features were in beta and encouraging feedback, and subsequent product changes (disablement, disclaimer, relabeling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image generation features and labelling intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple Intelligence can generate images on-device with the Image Playground app and create 'Genmoji' images; users can pick people in photos to have Genmoji generate images that resemble them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article mentions Image Playground's capabilities (styles like Animation and Sketch), integration with ChatGPT image-generation models, Notes/Image Wand accessibility on iPad, and references (in citations) to how Apple plans to label AI-generated images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing tools functionality and integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing tools powered by LLMs can proofread, rewrite, make text more friendly/concise/professional, and generate summaries, key points, tables, and lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes similarities to tools like Grammarly, and that in iOS 18.2 / macOS 15.2 a ChatGPT integration was added to Writing Tools through 'Compose' and 'Describe your change' features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release timeline and feature rollout (beta vs full launch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple Intelligence was launched for developers and testers on July 29, 2024, with partial releases on October 28, 2024 (iOS 18.1/macOS 15.1/iPadOS 18.1) and a stated plan to fully launch by 2026. The article includes a detailed release timeline of features by OS version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The release timeline lists which Apple Intelligence features arrived in which versions (e.g., Writing Tools, Siri overhaul, Image Playground, Visual Intelligence, Priority Notifications, Foundation Models Framework for Developers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Developer access to on-device foundation models (Foundation Models API)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple announced that its on-device foundation models will be available to third-party applications as part of the Foundation Models API, with support for structured data response and tool calling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes developer-facing access and capabilities (structured responses, tool calling) announced June 10, 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy claim for Visual Intelligence images (non-storage and access)
rubrics_metrics.description: When users take an image for Visual Intelligence features, 'The image taken is not stored on-device, and Apple claims they do not have access to the image either.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames this as Apple’s privacy claim about Visual Intelligence; the feature is intended to let people learn more about items faster and was later made available on various iPhone models starting with iOS 18.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance claims from Apple's human evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: According to a human evaluation done by Apple's machine learning division, the on-device foundation model beat or tied equivalent small models by Mistral AI, Microsoft, and Google, while the server foundation models beat the performance of OpenAI's GPT-3 while roughly matching the performance of GPT-4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports these comparative claims as Apple's human-evaluation results; they function as asserted performance benchmarks rather than independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing/advertising accuracy and legal accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal class action (Landsheft v. Apple Inc.) alleged false advertising and unfair competition regarding Apple's marketing that promised Apple Intelligence features at device release; the complaint claims many advertised AI capabilities did not exist at launch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article summarizes the complaint language, Apple’s motion to dismiss arguing only a small number of promised features were left out, and a joint notice of settlement in which parties reached an agreement in principle to resolve the matter on a classwide basis.
